title: Fear from the rod
hookLine: fear is born from taking up the rod; see the fish in shrinking water
tomorrow: The way to the far shore

lines: A POND AT THE END OF THE DRY SEASON.
cards: A pond at the end of a long dry season. The water has shrunk to a muddy patch in the middle, and the fish are crowded into it, flapping, pushing against each other for the last of it.

That image is at the heart of the Atthakavagga's final poem, Sutta Nipata 4.15. And unlike most discourses, it's spoken in the first person. The speaker tells what he saw, and how it shook him, before he ever found peace.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO TAKES UP THE ROD.
teach.b: The poem opens with a line that could stand alone: fear is born from the one who takes up the rod. Atta danda: the rod taken up, the stick picked up to strike. Look at people quarreling, the speaker says.
I saw people trembling, like fish in little water, set against one another, and fear came into me. The world seemed to have no core; every direction was shaken.
I looked for a place for myself and found none that wasn't already claimed. Seeing everyone in conflict to the end, I was disturbed. Then the turn.
I saw a dart, he says, hard to see, lodged in the heart. Pulled along by that dart, people run in every direction. Pull it out, and you don't run, and you don't sink.
First, the line about the rod cuts both ways: the one who picks up the stick creates fear in others, and also lives in fear. Second, the cause isn't finally the other fish.

It's the dart inside, the craving and grasping, that makes the pond feel so small. Commentaries set the poem during a quarrel between two clans, the Sakyans and the Koliyans, over the water of a river.
The poem itself names no one.

how: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions read the Attadanda Sutta as an account of the urgency, or samvega, that turns a person toward practice, and it is often cited in teaching on nonviolence.

games.q: you look out and see everyone in conflict, crowding like fish in a shrinking pond, and fear comes over you. what does the speaker of Sn 4.15 find next?
o: a dart, hard to see, lodged in the heart.
games.why: he sees the hidden dart that drives people every which way. pull it out, the poem says, and one neither runs nor sinks.

practice: Bring to mind a conflict you're part of, large or small: a sibling, a neighbor, a group chat, and ask what patch of water you're both fighting for: being right, being respected, being safe?
Look for the dart in your own chest, the wanting that keeps you flapping, without pulling hard. Just see it, and let the breath settle around it.

wordCard.voice: Attadanda, the rod taken up. The opening of Sutta Nipata 4.15: whoever takes up the stick to strike breeds fear, in others and in themselves.

orig.note: Pali attadanda: the rod taken up, the title of Sn 4.15. danda is a stick or rod.
